JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT

Rutgers University
Institute of Jazz Studies

Interview with
COZY COLE

Conducted by
BILL KIRCHNER
April 1980
Cassette #1

Prepared by:
STENOPHONIC TRANSCRIPTION SERVICES
Today is April 16, 1980.
That's right.
The day after taxes. Just got mine in yesterday.
Oh you did. Oh you were one of those last minute boys.
Mm hmm. And I'm getting money back.
Oh that's good.

We're sitting here in Bexley, Ohio, which is a suburb of Columbus and my name is Bill Kirchner and we're talking to one of the great jazz drummers probably, certainly one of the most versatile, and his name is Cozy Cole. I'm just going to cut this tape off for a minute.
And we're rolling once again. Cozy, to make things as easy as possible, why don't we just take things in more or less chronological order.
Okay, just as you want them, Bill.
Okay. Let's start out when you were, you know at the very beginning.

At the very beginning? Okay. Well, my school years, especially grammar school and high school was in Leonardo, New Jersey, which is a suburb of Asbury Park and Red Bank, New Jersey, Atlantic Highlands. I went
to school, high school there. Of course my mother died when I was in grade school; father died in high school.
Just to back track a step. We should probably get on the record that you were born in East Orange, New Jersey?
East Orange, New Jersey, that's correct.
October 17, 1909, right?
That is correct.
So far, John Chilton is right.
Yes.
I'm sorry to interrupt. So your mother died when, did you say?

My mother died while I was in grade school, and my father died when I was a freshman in high school and of course during my high school years I was taking manual training and I used to make drum sticks in manual training class and come home, and like the average kid, just beat all over your mother's chairs and tubs and everything.
I'm sure she loved that.
And, but my first inspiration to really see a drummer actually in person was Sonny Greer.
Oh.
He is from Long Branch or Seabright, if I'm not mistaken, and he was the only drummer then, especially Black drummer, working with all the white groups there in Jersey.
This is before he was with Duke?

Oh yeah, way before. And I was still in school when Sonny was playing around, so I used to see Sonny Greer and see him up there throwing his sticks around and just doing everything; he looked good and he was a great showman.
Oh, still is.
Yes. And that's who inspired me at the beginning was Sonny Greer.
Do you remember the names of any of the people he was working with?
No I don't. They were local people, local musicians from around Jersey.
Where were they playing at?

Well there was a fireman's hall where they used to play, the library, and different little halls around Red Bank, Asbury Park, Seabright, Long Branch, Kingsburgh, around Jersey there, and mostly all of those places where I would read about them playing, I would go and see Sonny.
What would they be doing, like singles?
What do you mean, singles?
Oh weddings, social receptions.
Oh yes, and public dances. Public dances and weddings, I imagine, but the times that I saw him mostly was at the public dances. Libraries and the different halls,
Fireman's Hall and different halls that they would rent for these occasions.
Did you get to meet him at that time?

Yes, I used to carry his drums from his gig, used to take them to my house, and then the next day I would get a bus and take them to his home, and believe it or not, when I first went to New York, oh it was around 1920, '29 around there, Sonny was with Duke Ellington.
Right.

Well I had to be introduced to Sonny all over again then, because I had grown up and he just looked at me and I said, I'm the kid that used to carry your drums from a gig or something, maybe you were busy, you know maybe with a chick or something, you wasn't married then, you know, so I would take your drums to my home and the next day deliver them to you. And Sonny used to give me fifty cents, a dollar to do that, which was great money in those days, and me being a kid, you know, I just thought that that was just beautiful.
That's quite a deal you got there.
Oh yes.
I think he got the better of it though.
And so that was my first inspiration was Sonny Greer.
Let me see, according to Chilton it said
two of your brothers were piano players, right?
Yes, Teddy and Jay, June, or Ruben. Teddy played with Roy Eldridge around Chicago for a while. Then Jay has played with oh, different groups around, this Miss Rhapsody in Newark, New Jersey.
What was that?

She was a singer, and he used to arrange for her and things, then Jay was with my band on the African tour and then at the Metropole when I was at the Metropole. And he's worked quite a bit around with different musicians, you know, free-lancing, but I can speak very well about him, the time that he spent with me; see he was with me oh four, five years with my band.
In the late '50s, early '60s.
Yes, then he also did the African tour with me.
Are they younger or older than you?
They were younger.
Are they both still alive?
No, Ruben passed on in 1975. And the rest of them are living, Ted
Teddy's alive.
Yeah, and then I have another youngest brother, Herbert. He plays drums also. He's in Asbury Park, New Jersey.
Does he play professionally?

Yes, sort of, he wasn't too interested in the drums, you know. He would play a little and then neglect them for a while and you just can't become professional when you put your instrument down like that and not play it. He wasn't interested in it that much, I would say. He'd play enough just to play and say that he was playing drums.
Three out of four in one family isn't bad.

Then I have a sister, she played piano. But not professionally. Played in church. She studied piano for years I guess this is when all of us were quite young. My father used to sing. He used to get us all around the piano and we would do a lot of, what would you call that, there's a word there that I want where we used to exercise-- syllabals. We used to exercise (SINGING) ....
Do re me fa sol.

Yeah, yeah, and believe it or not I used to sing soprano. You wouldn't believe that now because I have a bass voice, but all of us used to get around and sing things like that, syllables. And that's how, well I would say it was a musical family, really.
Sounds like it.
Yes. At the beginning, and of course I pursued mine and Ruben he did also, and also Ted. Herb is the only one that didn't take it too serious. My sister,
she played in churches and things of that nature. And that was it.
So how old were you when you started beating on your mother's furniture?

Oh well all right, say when I came out of high school I was 17, so in 1909, twelve years, that would make me how old, that would make me 9, 10, 11. No, 1909, so my first grade is when I was -- no it was in 1914, is that correct, yeah.
Then you would be how old?
Five.
Yeah, 1914.

1914. Well when I came out of high school, God, this has been so far back I forget. And so, I started really playing about two or three years after high school. As I told you, my father he died oh when I was a freshman in high school. So at the time I continued my education until I graduated from high school, and from that point on, all of the boys got together and worked after we came out of school, out of high school, we all got together and worked and helped my grandmother, which is the one that raised us after my mother and father died, to send our sister through school and we all worked and sent money home to our grandmother to send our sister through school, because she always used to tell us that it's much easier for you boys to make
it then a girl, you know, so we all got together and goodness, I went to New York at that time, I was a tinsmith at the beginning and then--
Did you apprentice?

Yes, yes, and I didn't stay with it too long because my first couple of days I had some nice clean overalls that I wore, and I came home that night and they were all full of that tar and everything, and I was saying God, there's got to be a much easier way to make a living than to fool with this. So anyway I didn't stay in that too long. Then from then on I was an errand boy, a shipping clerk, I was a porter, ran elevators around New York, things of that sort. When I came into music I was a head porter for New York Edison, to join Blanche Calloway's band, and I was afraid to quit this good job because as you know, working for New York Edison was a stable job, I mean it was consistent and what I'd heard about the music business, you know, you hit and run and you miss and you're gigging here and you're gigging there--
Something that never changes.

That's right. And so I've had an awful lot of experience other than playing drums, just doing little odd jobs on the outside, and then during my school years I worked on a farm, my brother and I. I can milk cows, plough and do all those sort of things.
Where was this at?

In Yorktown, New Jersey, that's in south Jersey. Yorktown, New Jersey, my aunt was there and we'd go there and work for the summer, during the summer months, and we enjoyed it, you know. We were young having a ball.
So you after high school had a lot of odd jobs.
Oh yes.
As you just mentioned. When did you start thinking about playing for a living?

All right, now let's see. During the time that I was doing that outside domestic, outside work, run the elevator, I was friends with a lot of boys that I'd met in New York and we used to fool around. Ukelele was very popular in those days. We used to stand around on the corners and play the ukulele, the Charleston was very popular, we used to get out there and dance and play our ukulele, and believe it or not, I used to dance in those years, they used to have chorus boys like they had chorus girls. Very prominent dancer around New York today, a boy by the name of Derby Wilson. Well he and I got an act together and I was dancing, he and I, Cole and Wilson, and we were tap dancers. But, Bill, everybody I would run into or saw in the street then could dance better than I

could. Everybody, and of course Bill Robinson was very popular during that time, and I said oh God, it just doesn't take anything, any education at all to get out here and dance, because there's a son of a gun over there that hasn't even been to grade school and can outdance everybody, so then is when I started to study, and my first teacher, I was recommended through a friend of mine, to a drummer that was working in the pit at the Lincoln Theatre in New York, 135th and Lenox Avenue', his name was Charlie Brooks, and I started taking lessons with him, which was oh a dollar a lesson. He lived at 3 West 135th Street, and it was a walkup, about three flights up. His wife played drums, also his son.
That's a nice walk for a drummer with all of his equipment.

Oh yes, yes. But when I was taking lessons, see, I didn't have to bring my drums. He had the practice pad and things up there, you know, so that was my first teacher was Charlie Brooks. Then I hated to go up there for lessons for the simple reason his wife could play drums and also his son, and my time to take a lesson, they would always be home and sitting right in the same room where I would be taking my lessons. Well if I'd do something wrong, well he would reprimand me and there they'd be sitting there, you know. I just felt bad about that, you know, and I just hated to go there and take lessons if they were there.
How old were you when this was taking place?
Oh, say I was out of high school a couple of years. This was about 1928, I'd say, around there, '27 or '28. It's around that, that era, '27, '28, when I just started.
Okay, so you were getting your technical thing together at that point.

Then, at that point. See, he was my first teacher. Of course from then on, there on, oh goodness, I've had any number of teachers, you know. I studied with Billy Gladstone, he was at Radio City Music Hall.
Very famous pit--

Oh yeah, very. Yes. Then I studied tympani with Sol Goodman, he was with the Philharmonic Symphony. And then I studied drums with Freddy Albright and quite oh, I studied xylophones with Milton Schlesinger, he's the one who used to do all the Lucky Strike Hours and things like that. So that's when I really started to get my feet into it, really, you know, and down to hard study was during those years, those gentlemen. Now of course with Billy Gladstone, I studied with him a couple of years. Shelly Mann, I was studying with him at the same time. And I was busy with Louie all the time, and so a lot of times I had to quit studying and then go on the road with either band, whether it was with Cab Calloway or any band
that I would be with and that's why I wasn't consistent with a lot of the teachers, because I was in and out of town all the time.
I guess when you become a working professional, that's the way it is.
Yeah, yeah, it's hard to stay in one place all the time because you've got to make some kind of bread in order to survive.
And pay the teacher.
Yeah, that's right, that's right. So all those years were very exciting, I would say, to me, I loved them. I had a lot of fun.
It says in Chilton's book that your family moved to New York in 1926.
Not my family. It was me.
Just you.
Yeah, just me.
Okay, so that would have made you 17.
Yeah, about 17, 18 years old.
That's after you got out of high school.
Yes.
And it says that you became a professional in 1928.
Well, then's when I joined the union, 1928. After I joined the union, that period, there were house
parties.
Rent parties.

House rent parties, that's right. Twenty-five cents admission there in New York. Well there used to be a little old piano player around there, any number of piano players that I worked with, Bobby Clarke, Willy Gant.
Oh yeah, Willy the Tiger.
Yeah, yeah, Willy Gant, we used to work these house parties. Now I guess you could call that professional playing, couldn't you?
Certainly.
Anyway, we had a gig we used to do on 135th Street which was 305 West 135th Street.
Right near Charlie Brooks's place.

No, Charlie was at 3 West 135th which was at Fifth Avenue. 305 was across 8th Avenue and St. Nicholas, 8th and St. Nicholas, 305, and it was a walkup five flights, yeah five flights, and every Saturday night Bobby Clarke and I had this little gig up there, we'd go five dollars, five dollars, and at that time all the drummers were using was 28-inch bass drums which were big. Yeah, of course today they're 20 inches you know, 20, 22, normal size. Well anyway I used to carry these drums up these five flights, get up there and set them up
and it was my first full set of drums.
What brand were they, just out of curiosity?
I think they were Ludwigs. I think, I'm not sure. Ludwigs or Slingerland.

Anyway, inside the bass drum, they used to have electric light bulbs that would go on and off and on the head was a picture of Rudolph Valentino and Pola Negro, painted on your bass drum head. So I used to get on this gig a little early and set my drums up and plug it in and look at the lights go on and off, you know, about an hour before we'd even start playing, and we would get, like I told you, five dollars a night, sometimes not that if business wasn't good, but we were young and having a ball, having fun, and we'd get a meal, pig's feet or chittlings or whatever they had, fried chicken, and if they didn't give you the five dollars, when you finished well, Cozy, here's three, and next Saturday or come back Tuesday we'll give you the two, or next Saturday we'll make up the difference. Well that was all right with us you know, because--
Did they always pay up?

Always paid up, you know. Sometimes they were a little long trying to get that bread together, but we'd always get it, and I would say that was the beginning of my professional playing then. Then by being around with musicians, around the band box, there used to be a place

named the Band Box, a rhythm club where all the musicians used to hang out. Well when I was working these house parties, see I was during that professionally every day in the week, because while I was playing the house parties I still had an every day gig, running elevators and like that, but during the day I would always go around where the musicians used to hang, which was the Band Box, the Rhythm Club and sit around and listen to them talk, listen to them rehearse, until time to go to work, and time to go to work, I'd leave and go on my little gig that I was going on, run the elevator, porter or shipping clerk or whatever. So this afternoon I was around listening to them rehearse and Jelly Roll Morton came by the rehearsal and he wanted a drummer. Well there were quite a few drummers around at that time but Jelly, everybody just loved Jelly Roll Morton at the time, but Jelly was a little long in paying their bread, you know, after you would do a recording date, he would take about a month to pay you and I guess a lot of those guys just shied away from Jelly, not that they didn't like him, but they liked their money as soon as they finished the job.
I heard that some guys were just turned off by his bragging. Is that true?
I don't think so, because fellas used to sit around and egg Jelly on, they used to love to hear him argue-- brag like that, you know, and he and Chick Webb used

to get into the darnedest arguments you ever heard and the guys used to sit around there and just egg him on and he would go. So anyway, Jelly said 'Where can I get a drummer?' Well the musicians around the club didn't know me by name, they just said there's a kid over there I think plays drums. So he came over and approached me, 'Do you play drums?' I says yeah. 'Who'd you ever work with?' That's when I started lying you know, because God, Jelly Roll Morton, I'd been reading about him, I looked at Jelly, I said, Man, this is it, Jelly Roll Morton asking me to make a recording date with him? And I started lying, telling him some old jive, names, man, all around Jersey, that I'd worked with. He said where are your drums? I said they're at home. So he had a big car and he says, 'Okay, we'll go around and get them and we'll make the recording date.' I said okay. Scared to death. This was my first recording date, first time I'd ever worked with a number of musicians other than a piano player. Those house rent parties, you know, just a piano player. This was around 1929, '28. So anyway, I went by my house and we picked up the drums and we did a recording date, and luckily I did a good job, because all I had to do was keep time and 'Load of Coal' (Lode of Cole) I think I had a four-bar break on some of the numbers, or something like that. Anyway, I made out all right, and Jelly paid me my money right away, and that is the only time my longest acquaintance with Jelly was on that recording

date, which was two hours and maybe two hours prior to the date getting the drums and going to the recording studio. So people come up to me today and say, Well, Cozy, you knew Jelly Roll? I said yeah, I knew him, but I didn't know Jelly that well. And so they said, oh goodness, I know you've got to be ninety years old to know Jelly Roll Morton. I said no, I said it was one of those things, when I worked with Jelly I was just a little kid, you know, and that was my experience with Jelly. Of course after the recording date then I'd see him on the streets or in the club, he would remember me, and start talking.
I've got in front of me a Xerox of the discography--
Oh yea, what was that?
That lists all the titles that you made with him.
Oh yeah, what were they?
Let's see. First session is Jelly Roll Morton and his Red Hot Peppers from March 5, 1930 with Jelly Roll, Ward Pinkett and another on trumpets--do you remember who the other one was?
No, I don't.
Wilbur de Paris, Ernie Bullock or Jerry Blake on clarinet and bass clarinet. Bernard Addison.
Bernard Addison, guitar, yeah.
Billy Taylor.
Bass.
He's still alive and living in Virginia.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.

And yourself. And those titles are "Each Day," "If Someone Would Only Love Me," "That Will Never Do," and "I'm Looking for a Little Bluebird." And the second session which is June 2, 1930, is Jelly Roll, again Ward Pinkett and another on trumpet, Geechie Fields on trombone, Happy Caldwell on clarinet, Joe Thomas on alto sax, Walter Thomas on clarinet and baritone, Lee Blair on banjo, Billy Taylor once again on bass, and you; and those are "Oil Well," two takes of "Load of Coal," and "Crazy Chords," and "Primrose Stomp." Any of those ring a bell?
Yeah, "Primrose Stomp." It rings a bell.
I've got a cassette with some of those on it, I'll play it later.
Okay, I'd like to hear "Primrose Stomp," yeah.
So you did two different sessions with him.
Yes. Do you know, I hardly remember the second one? But--
That was the one with "Load of Coal" on it.
Yes. Was that the second one?
Right.
Mm hmm. That's a long while ago.
Oh sure, fifty years.
Yeah, fifty years.
You were talking about the Band Box and the Rhythm Club. Does the Ellington and Henderson bands used to hang out there?

Oh yeah. All bands. I'll tell you what happened at that club. At the time, Fletcher Henderson was working at the Roseland. Duke was at the Cotton Club I think. I just forget where the Dorseys were playing and Paul Whitman and all the white bands, they were all downtown. But, when everybody would finish work, they would all come up to the Band Box. See the Band Box was their earlier name, later on it was named the Rhythm Club, so that was a regular hangout for all musicians, wherever they were working. So, Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Lou Russell, Lucky Millinder, Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey, Jack Teagarden, Artie Shaw, Paul Whitman, all of them they used to come right up there to that Rhythm Club and sit up there and sometimes they'd play cards, gamble, and they served meals, they would eat. Sometimes they'd have some of the darnedest jam sessions you've ever heard of. Right there. And when...
... cutting contest.
Oh yeah, yeah, Benny Carter can tell you the same thing about that era. And well, see on a Sunday night

I think it was when the Band Box or the Rhythm Club would really jump. Because all the bands used to come up there and eat and sit down and play or listen to different musicians play and the reason I mention Sunday night because that would be the night that there would be a breakfast dance at Small's Paradise. Charlie Johnson's band was there, and there was a great drummer in that band, his name is George Stafford.
Benny Carter was there right?
Yeah, right, Benny Carter was in that band. Wilbur de Paris, Sidney de Paris, Cy St. Claire, bass. Benny Waters, tenor saxophone.
He's still around right?

Yeah he's in Paris, yeah. And that's when we would all leave the Band Box, the Rhythm Club and go to Small's, because the breakfast dance didn't start until about six o'clock in the morning, and we would be in there from six o'clock until about eleven o'clock Monday morning, or Monday afternoon, or six o'clock until about eleven, twelve o'clock noon Monday, one or two o'clock Monday afternoon. Then we had really a ball. And then there was another place that used to have contests, big bands, battle of the big bands. What was the name of that place?
The Savoy?
No. Rockland Palace. 155th and 8th Avenue. Those were something else. They always used to have a battle
of music up there with Charlie Johnson and Chick Webb's band. But where they used to have some good battles was at the Savoy. There was Chick Webb, Benny Goodman, Cab, all the bands.
Well, Chick had the house band, right?

Yeah, yeah, at the Savoy. Ella was with the band. That was a great band, Chick Webb's band at that time. Sandy Williams on trombone, Taft Jordan, Wayman Carver, Elmer Williams, tenor saxophone, Wayman Carver was playing flute. I think Pauley was in that band too for a while. But that was a great band. Chick and Ella, oh goodness, I worked opposite Chick's band up there while I was with Willie Bryant. We worked opposite Chick's band for a year, a year and a half. Benny Carter was in the band then with Willie Bryant, Benny Carter, Teddy Wilson.
Before we get too much into that, let me ask you one thing about Wilbur Sweetman.
Wilbur Sweetman, okay.
That was even before you went with Jelly Roll right? Or recorded with Jelly Roll.
No, no, this was after Jelly.
We'll have to tell Mr. Chilton that. He says with Wilbur Sweetman, circa 1928.
Now wait a minute, let me see. This was after Jelly. This was after Jelly.
Okay.
Well I'll tell you about Wilbur Sweatman. Now this was my first big band active playing.
How big a band was it?
Ten pieces. Ten pieces.
Which was standard size at the time.
Yes. Turn that off for a second.

Let me just add before you get back to it. Cozy just showed me a photograph he has up on the wall of him with the Wilbur Sweatman band in 1930 in New York and two photographs as a matter of fact. I'm sorry, go ahead.

And of course that was my first band, actual professional playing. Well there was a little riff that he had a couple of girls with him that danced. He had a regular show. And of course with the band he had these little acts, two girls dancing, another boy dancing, and there was a little tom-tom rhythm that used to go boom-di-di-di-di-di, boom didi-didi di-bam (EXAMPLE) Well at home, I could play the devil out of that doggone thing, because I would practice it at home, I wanted this job so bad, you know ... And our first gig was at a theatre in Union, New Jersey and when the curtain would open, that would be the first rhythm that was heard, and I had to set it (EXAMPLE). Well when that curtain opened up I was doing (EXAMPLE) and Wilbur Sweatman would look at me, those pretty chorus girls would look at me, For Christ sake, get

that drummer off there, I just couldn't do it, you know, I was stage fright, stage fright. So anyway, everybody as you saw in the picture was older than I was, and they'd say, oh kid, for Christ sake, you can do that, come on here with me. And I didn't drink. Here, take a little drink. And I'd take a little drink and you know after that little thing going and come back for the next show and do the same thing and mess up again. So I didn't stay with Sweatman too long. I was with Sweatman oh, about a week and a half. He gave me my two-week notice and fired me on account of that. And I just couldn't do it, which inspired me and made me want to go ahead and really do it, because that's very embarrassing, I mean to get fired out of a band, and that inspired me to really go ahead and study the drums. Then's when I really got down to business. And Wilbur Sweatman before he died, long before he died, we used to talk about it all the time, about how I messed up and he fired me. He said, 'Cozy, I hated to do it,' he said, 'because you're a nice guy, I liked you,' he said, 'but you just couldn't get that rhythm together,' and I couldn't. And those girls, you know, they were back there, oh get rid of that drummer, he's messing up our dancing.
They depended on you.
Oh of course. I didn't blame them. So that was my first job that I got fired off of. That one.
Then--
And that was after Jelly Roll.

Yeah, that was after Jelly Roll. Then I did another little thing, up around the same Band Box and Rhythm Club, it was a great arranger around there and he used to do a lot of dancing school gigs. Name was Charlie Skeets.
Skeets?

Skeets. S K E E T S.* Well he had this audition to do downtown in a beautiful dancing school and I was on drums. Russell Procope was on alto saxophone. John Kirby was on bass. It was down around 48th Street, the Star Ballroom or something like that. Well anyway, Charlie Skeets had this little arrangement by Archie Bleyer.
One of the great stock arrangement writers.

That's right, by Archie Bleyer. And it was 'No Parking.' And it was very simple. I think it was a down beat on the drums--boom, and then just about three bars and then the saxophones would come in. I messed that up. I messed that up, and all it was was nerves. So they lost the audition on account of me messing up that audition. Procope and I talk about that today. I just saw Procope about a year ago, he was working with Brooks Kerr and Sonny Greer.
Were you in New York?
Yeah, I was in New York. They were in at 61st and 1st Avenue and Procope and I talk about that.
Was Sonny Greer still with them?

I think so, I think so. And so that day everybody left that audition, left me there with those drums, and I had to walk from 48th Street uptown with these drums. because I didn't have a nickel to come, because we all came down in cars.
So you were stranded.

And that was my second experience. My third experience was another in a band in a dancing school in the Bronx, Sylvester Lewis, trumpet player, and I went up there and that is the last time I was fired off a gig, off that job. The reason I was fired off that one is because I couldn't keep good time. A number would start .... by the time I got to the end I was here .... the bass player and all used to get on me, the trumpet player, everybody. But I just couldn't keep good time. I'd practice with a metronome but up there, imagine, I would get excited.
Still nervous.

That's right. So that was my experience of getting fired out of Wilbur Sweatman's band, messing up Charlie Skeet's audition, and getting out of Sylvester Lewis' band for not keeping time, and from then on is when I really started putting my thinking cap on and started working hard, trying to develop something. But that kind of experience, I mean it does you all the good in the world.

I mean it did me good, it made me realize that you know, the more you study, the more you find out you don't know and you've got to keep on studying, you know, and just don't get brought down because you got fired, I guess a lot of guys got fired off the first gigs that they ever went on, you know.
Or should have been.
Yeah. Or should have been, that's right.
One thing that just occurred to me. How did you get your nickname?

Cozy? In high school. See, I love athletics, the hundred-yard dash, pole vaulting, broad jumping, football, baseball and basketball, but I just loved football. Well, in high school, you become acquainted with different people in other high schools. So this friend of mine was in another high school in Red Bank. His name was B. Z. Runyon, big guy. You know how kids always attach a nickname to somebody who's big. Well we used to call him Beanzy Runyon. Well he and I hit it off right away. We got to be good friends. So we used to sit around and talk football and things like that. And different moves, different passes and everything. Well this particular day afternoon, we were playing against his school, so we were up there playing, I was a sophomore at the time and the quarterback threw me a forward pass and I caught it beautiful. The whole class got up and applauded for me you know, man I was running down the field. I happened

to look up at that line and saw Beanzy coming. And Beanzy is big period. And with all that regalia on, the shoulder pads and all that, he looked like a mountain coming after you. So Beanzy knew every step that I was going to take and I knew that. But he tackled me but not hard. It was afterwards, that scrimmage, all on top of you. Anyway he tackled me and he dislocated my shoulder and they had to carry me off the field, they brought a stretcher on there, and they had to carry me off the field. So from that day on, when they were carrying me off, I said will this is my last day playing football because I never will be able to play drums with my ribs broken, my hands and things like that. Now as far as the name is concerned, out on the practice field, like he'd be out there practicing and let anybody throw you a forward pass would call you by your last name. Colezy. Well during the course of the practicing they weren't particular about diction, just Cozy, and that's how it started. So it was two last names. It sounded funny at first, but now my first name as you know is William. Somebody call me Willy or Bill, it sounds funny. I'm so used to hearing Cozy.
Well let's see, you just told about how you struck out on the three different gigs, and when did you start to have a better track record?

Well the better track record started when I went with Blanche Calloway. Then's when I started to realize what it was all about. Ben Webster was in the band, Edgar Battle, Clyde Hart, and we'd start playing shows. Blanche Calloway.
And that was in 1931?
On the cassette I have with me, I've got a recording of "Just a Crazy Song."
By Blanche?
By Blanche. Remember that?

Oh boy. Yeah. I'll tell you about Blanche Calloway's band. Of course she, Cab was very popular at the time, so Blanche Calloway was his sister, so she was popular right along with him. But we had a fairly nice band, a good band, but it wasn't a standard good band like McKinney's Cotton Pickers or Chick Webb or something like that. We'd always be up in one of those band spaces, playing the battle of music, you know. All we had was about three or four arrangements that we played.
And the rest were heads?

Yeah it was heads you know and we enjoyed it you know, young, you know and enjoyed playing. One time, we played a battle of music with Duke in Philadelphia and everybody knew us around Philly and liked us, the audience

wouldn't let us get off the stand. And Duke come on. They kept applauding, you know, for us to come back and do an encore. All we had was about two or three numbers, I think our best arrangement was on "Trees" (HUMMING)
Who did that?
Clyde Hart made the arrangement of that.
I read not too long ago in Downbeat an interview with Vic Dickenson who was on Blanche's band later than you were.
Yeah, yeah, I wasn't with the band then.
And he said something to the effect--I can't quote exactly--he said something to the effect that Blanche had a band as good as any man's.

She had a good band if we could play. See here's the thing about Blanche's band. They had some very good players in there. Boy by the name of Booker Pittman on the clarinet and saxophone, very fast tongue for tonguing alto and clarinet; Ben Webster, very good; Edgar Battle, trumpet. Well see, Blanche would be in front of the band and we used to do a number like "I Need Loving," (HUMMING). Well anyway, Blanche would be in front of the band dancing. Well, if Ben had a solo or any one of the musicians had a solo to play, Blanche would still be out there dancing, selling the band. Well while she's dancing and kicking her legs up in the air, kicking her legs up dancing, I had to

catch her on the cymbals. Well see, well that's very unprofessional with Ben Webster taking a solo and you're up there trying to catch Blanche Calloway when she's kicking her legs upin the air on the cymbal. You know that was one of the troubles.
I'm sure Ben didn't appreciate that.
Oh no, but he couldn't do anything about it because it was Blanche's band. That's what she wanted, you know. So.
Did he get mad at you?

Ben? No, because see he knew what I was doing. He'd try to tell Blanche and Blanche would say, 'well, you know this is my band and if you don't like it, you know, there's somebody around the corner that'll take your place,' you know. And one of those things. But we were all together for a long while, but all in all it was a good band when they'd really get down and play. We had some good head arrangements, Joe Keyes was in there, very good trumpet player.
You were with her for a couple of years, right?
A couple of years, because after her was when I joined Benny Carter. About '33, '34, something like that.
I'm forgetting, were you on the record that Benny made of Spike Hughes' arrangements, the British arranger?
No. I never recorded with Benny.
That band has a reputation today of being very much a musician's band. Something that musicians loved to hear but that never was all that successful. That's your experience.

Oh yeah, yeah. Well Benny had arrangements then, I think it's around that same time, an arrangement on "Sleep," do you remember that arrangement? That was a very good arrangement, Benny Carter's band.
He recorded it later.
Yeah, yeah, "sleep."
Were you on that one or not?
No, no. I didn't record with Benny.
That's right, you said you didn't. Because I remember hearing the recording. I think he did it maybe about two or three years after you were with him.
Probably so.
So who was on the band when you were with Benny?

With Benny? Well, Teddy Wilson, Keg Johnson, Johnny Russell, Glyn Paque Johnny Russell was a tenor player, Glyn Paque was alto and Benny. Bill Dillard trumpet, Bill Coleman trumpet. Fella by the name of Link, trumpet. He had three trumpets. Trombones was Big Green, trombone, Dicky Wells and Keg Johnson. The rhythm section was Ernest Hill, Lawrence Lucie, guitar, Teddy Wilson and me.
That was a great band.
Oh yeah, that was a good band. That was a good band.
Benny played a lot of lead alto.
Lead alto and trumpet sometimes. And trumpet.
Where did you work with him?

Oh, we were the first band that played the Apollo theatre in the pit and on stage. Then we worked in the Ubangi Club. It was later named the Ubangi Club, it was the old Connie's Inn ... Then I worked the Lafayette Theatre with Benny and different theatres.
Did you stay in New York or did you travel at all?
Well we stayed in New York when we worked in New York. Now when we played Philadelphia, Washington, we stayed wherever the engagement was.
But since that was the Depression, it was pretty hard to get that band working I'm told.

Yes, it was, but we seemed to manage somehow. I mean, the money wasn't that great, you know, but it didn't take too much money then to live. And of course everybody just loved working with Benny. On the count, well he made such beautiful charts, everybody loved to play them. See, that's the thing, you'd almost work for Benny Carter for nothing, and go there and play and listen to that good
music. Then to think about the money too much.
What was the audience's reaction to the band usually?

They loved it, they loved it. They loved it. I guess the only reason why Benny wasn't like a Duke Ellington or something like that he was the personality or something, but I don't know you know how they was dealing and wheeling in those days, stealing those managers and things you know. Benny wasn't going for that, you know, and so he made it all right, but he never made it real big.
He was never as much of a showman as Duke.
No, no.
Or Lundsford.
Lundsford, no, that's right, or Don Redman, or like that you know. Benny Carter was great.
So you were with him it says in Chilton in late 1933 and '34.
'34, that's right.
And then you went to Willie Bryant?
I think so.
Willie Bryant, '35, '36.
Yeah, yeah, Willie Bryant. With Willie Bryant.
Who was basically a singer, right?
A singer and a great showman, a great showman.

You know we worked at the Savoy, that's where we worked, opposite Chick Webb's band. Then in the Apollo, any time Willie wanted to go to the Apollo Theatre, we'd always be in there. Then of course the Savoy, we were always there. And the Howard Theatre, the Lincoln Theatre, the Pearl Theatre in Philly, the Lincoln in Philly, the Howard in Washington, the Royal Theatre in Baltimore, and mostly our longest engagements were at the Savoy. We were there, oh, for months at a time.
When you did the circuits, how did you travel? By train or bus?
Bus. Bus. At one time, you know, one of the manager's of the Savoy, Charles Buchanan, he and Moe Gayle and all of them got together and they had a five-band tour.
Five bands together?
Yes, five bands together, which was Johnson's Happy Pals, Zack White.
Which was from Cincinnati.
Cincinnati. Benny Moton.
From Kansas City.
That's right. Chick Webb.
From New York.
And Blanche Calloway.
Also from New York.
Five bands, and we traveled by bus then.
One time we made a jump from Baltimore, Maryland--from Kansas City to Baltimore, Maryland. And we got in Baltimore just in time to change clothes on the bus.
Did you say you were all on one bus?
Oh no, they had five buses. Five different buses. Oh no. No, five different buses. We were on that tour, oh, about eighteen days.
What year was that, do you remember?
Around then, '33.
The early '30s.
Yeah, five-band tour. They don't talk too much about that in any of these jazz magazines. A lot of them I don't think knew about it too much.
The first I've ever heard of it.
Yeah, five-band tour. Boy that was something.
Was it pretty successful?
Yeah, it was very good, very good.
The audiences liked it.
Oh yeah, loved it. Loved it. Benny Moton, Chick Webb, they were the best bands. Of course Zack Whyte had a good band then. I think Vic Dickenson was with Zack Whyte at the time, Vic Dickenson and Sy.
Sy Oliver.
Yeah, I think they were with the band. I know that we played a battle of music with Zack Whyte in
Pottstown, Pennsylvania, and Vic Dickenson and Sy Oliver was with that band. Was with Zack Whyte at the time.
That's when you were Blanche Calloway.
Blanche Calloway.
You were talking about Willie Bryant being a great showman.
Oh yeah. Yeah, Willie was a great showman. Willie Bryant could stop a show with his showmanship. See, Willie Bryant, you couldn't tell whether he was white or black. But he was black.
Was he mulatto?

I imagine you would say that. But anyway he had that little complex. A white audience, he would bomb because people would look at him and say what the hell is he, white or black, and he knew that. And he couldn't work in front of them good.
He got nervous.

Yeah, that's right. A black audience, he'd break up. Let his hair all fall down, you know, those chicks looking at him, screaming. A white audience Willie would bomb in front of, just couldn't work them. Now he would go but not as well.
That was mostly in New York that you worked with him?
Yeah, I'd say mostly.
Where?
Well the Savoy we worked, then we went to Buffalo, we worked at the--can't think of the club-- anyway, they had an NBC wire....

After Willie. Now, I met Stuff in Buffalo, at the time I was with Willie Bryant. We was working this club in Buffalo that I couldn't think of the name, and Stuff is out of Buffalo, that's his home. Buffalo and so Stuff asked me would I like to join the band, so I said yes, and then's when I joined the band, out of Willie Bryant's band, I would join Stuff at the Onyx Club on 52nd Street. There I stayed, oh goodness, I was with Stuff quite a while till I joined Cab Calloway. And then oh goodness, all during that time that I was with Stuff, is when I started to do records with everybody, you know like with Bunny Berigan, Dick McDonna and Carl Kriss..
Mildred Bailey.
Mildred Bailey, Red Norvo, Joe Marsella, oh yeah, Red Norvo, Lionel, Ella, of course Sarah, Sarah Vaughn, the Andrews Sisters, yeah, I did a lot of recordings.
How were those record dates arranged? Did they just tell you to show up at the studio at such and such a time?

Yeah, well they would come by the club you know wherever you'd be working and they say 'would you like to do a record date with me next Monday or whenever'. And you would look at your schedule. Yes. And they'd tell you just what studio and time and that was it. You'd go do it. It was just a record date.
Were the sessions three hours then?
Three hours then.
Same as now.
Yeah, same as now, sometimes you'd have to
four tunes in the three hours.
What was recording scale?
I think it was then $45.00, something like that, $50.00. I forget the exact amount then. But it was good money then.
Sure.
It was good money then.

I'm looking at the Discography for Stuff Smith. On the tape I've got a few things you did with him. Some of those things are showing up now on some of those jazz records that have been coming out in the past couple of years that all have marijuana related songs on it.
Oh yes, 'Dream about Reefers,' 'You'se A Viper.'

Yeah, 'You'se A Viper,' 'Here Comes the Man With the Jive,' things like that. You did those in 1936. And the only musician on there beside you and of course Stuff who really has any kind of a reputation was Jonah Jones.
Yeah, the rest of them Mack Walker, Bobby Bennett and Clyde Hart, wasn't it, or Sherman.
James Sherman.
James Sherman, yeah, mm hmm.
Jonah plays very well.
Oh yeah, oh yeah, yes. Jonah's a good player.
How did you get along with Stuff? He was quite a character.

Oh yeah, oh yeah. Stuff was just great. Stuff didn't do any harm to anybody but himself. He was just great, you know. We got along swell. Got along swell. He's one of the greatest jazz violinists I've ever heard in my life. He and Joe Venuti, they were just great. Yeah, I got along wonderful with Stuff, and in the band, all the guys got along with Stuff.

No, a lot of times we would rehearse. It's a funny thing, this is a little something about Stuff that everybody knew Stuff used to drink a lot, you know, but you'd never see Stuff drunk so he couldn't play. So one night we were all up on the bandstand and things weren't sounding just right, you know. So Jonah and I used to sit right next to him, you know, sort of where you could turn around and say something to me and Jonah. So then, he says, 'Are we sounding all right tonight?' you know. And Jonah and I said 'Yes, Stuff, it sounds good.' So Stuff would look at me and say, 'Cozy, are you high?' I'd say 'no.' 'Jonah, are you high?' 'No.' Well then Stuff turned around and said 'Oh man, that's what wrong, everybody ain't high by 12:00 I'm going to fine you five dollars.' And anyway--
(LAUGHTER) High or drunk?
Drinking. So anyway, there used to be a bar right at the corner of 52nd and Sixth Avenue. All

the boys used to stop by and have a little taste, everybody. Roy Eldridge, Charlie Shavers, Kirby, Maxine Sullivan, Billie Pearl Bailey, everybody stop by, fifteen cent a drink, you know, go over there and get a little taste before coming to work. Well the White Rose was about from here to that tree away from the Onyx Club. Well in the White Rose it's close.
That was on the corner of 52nd and 6th.

Yeah, Sixth Avenue. And the Onyx was right around the corner. First club. So by being all fenced in there, you could smell all that whiskey on your clothes, you know. So anyway, like, we'd all meet there at the White Rose, come and have a taste, some of us wouldn't. But anyway, when you would come in the club on your clothes you could smell maybe a little whiskey or something, the aroma from the whiskey and all. So they used to say, 'uh uh, it's going to be a good night tonight 'cause they all high. Wait until about 12 or one o'clock and boy it's going to be a good night.' And just as sure as ever, around twelve, one o'clock it was a good night, everybody up there just high--not drunk you know, just Stuff he's high, and the higher he would get, the better he could play. Yeah, the higher Stuff would get, the better he could play. And as far as the tunes are concerned, we used to to like

"Crescendo on Drums," we had a rehearsal that day, and Stuff just started, he'd say okay, Cozy you do this, Jonah you do this, and we do this, and we just started in playing and then we got to further on in the piece, and things started and held together, and said oh yeah, we'll keep that in, that sounds good, and that's how it came about, just like that.
That's the same one that you later recorded with Cab.
Cab, yeah, "Crescendo on drums."
So you originated that when you were with Stuff.
Yeah, with Stuff, yeah. Stuff Smith, "Crescendo on Drums," (HUMMING) Remember it?
Yeah. As a matter of fact I've got the record with me.
"Crescendo on Drums."
So is that when you first really got in with Jonah Jones.

I met Jonah as I told you when I was in Buffalo with Stuff. Stuff Smith, then's when I met Jonah and Stuff was there in Buffalo. In 1936 wasn't it, somewhere around there. Yeah, thens when I first met them and then we used to jam together all up around there, all together.
So you were mostly at the Onxy with Stuff.

Yeah, mostly, yeah. Of course I worked in the Onyx, there were different groups, Hot Lips Paige, I was there with Hot Lips; then I had a little trio in there, my trio with Hank D'Amico and John Guarnieri. See, then's when I was on staff at CBS.
That was in the '40s.
Yeah.
I met Johnny Guarnieri a couple of years ago in Toronto.
Yeah, who was he with?

Yeah, Johnny's a great pianist. Yeah, he can mimic Fats Waller down to the nth degree.
Yeah, really small hands, too, for a piano player.
Yeah, Johnny can play. Johnny's a good piano player. Tell you something about that. See we were on staff up there with Raymond.
Raymond Scott.

Mm hmm. So they wanted a trio in the Onyx. The manager approached me and I took a trio to the Onyx which consisted of Johnny, Hank D'Amico and me. We went in there. Hank was, he wasn't a alcoholic but every

So when I got paid I'd give Johnny his envelope, and when with Hank, I'd say wait a minute, Hank, we've got to figure up all these tabs that you have had. But that was a good trio. Where? At the Onyx?
Yeah.

Somebody got up and stood in front of-- I've got that somewhere in one of my scrap books--where he punched some guy in the eye for standing in front of him. He said, Man, I want to listen to Cozy's trio. So that was a great gig there, I worked in there with Billie Holiday, Hot Lips Page.
This is in the late '30s?
Mm hmm. Hot Lips Page, Billie.

Oh great, great. Any with Lester Young?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, made some with Lester.
Those were put together pretty casually, right?

Yeah, yeah, but that "Miss Brown to You," boy, was really a swinging note thing. I've heard the tune, and I've heard Lionel do it, but I haven't heard that particular record.
"Sweethearts on Parade." Chu Berry. Great record.
And Chu was a great player.
Oh boy, he could swing, that's the thing, see just anything. Tell you what we did. We were working the Palomar Theatre in Seattle, Washington, with Cab. And

this woman came by, she owned this club, and wanted if Chu and I could come on out there and play. You know, jam, which is all right, we didn't think too much of jamming in those days. Cozy Cole endorses such and such drums.

That's right, and you don't know anything about it. (Louis)

in the trees, son of a guns up there sitting with their little tapes and things going, and they were going to tape the whole concert if he didn't know it. He tore down all that and then we went on and started playing. Oh yeah. You've got to really know what's going on in order to, you know ....
Bootlegging isn't new.
Oh no, and what're you going to do about it? You can't do anything about it. You're over here and they're over there.
The only thing you can do is invest money in a lawyer and it's not worth the trouble.
No, no because you may end up with nothing.
Or more in legal fees then you get back.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. So you've got to be very very careful. And I imagine there isn't too much of that going on now, you know, too many musicians are hep to what's going on.
