Milt claimed that he did it. But that Cab blamed Dizzy.

Yeah, because Diz was always up there fooling around. And so one word led on to another after the curtain closed. 'You're a damn liar it wasn't me.' 'You're a damn liar it was you,' and one word led on to another, it wasn't that severe about all that cutting and all that, because Benny Payne stopped it you know.
Dizzy didn't pull a knife.

No, not all that. It wasn't that. Maybe Diz had a knife in his hand, but it wasn't all that. But you know how they can build up a big story. And that was it. And Diz was fired. And the next week we were at the Apollo Theatre and Diz was sitting right up in the front row.

I guess we've kind of eased into Cab's band without trying to. Before we do that let me take it back a step to the small group records that you made, with Chu. Let's see, I'll just read off the names of the guys who were on there. Maybe that might jiggle a few memories for you. It was Chu, Hot Lips Paige, George Matthews on Trombone, Buster Bailey, Horace Henderson, Lawrence Lucie, Israel Crosby and you, and that was in 1937. You did 'Now You're Talking My Language,' 'Indiana,' 'Too Marvelous for Words,' and 'Limehouse Blues.' Do you remember anything from those?

Yeah I remember them, they were all good sessions. It wasn't anything outstanding about them, but as a whole they were all good sessions, you know, and you always looked forward in doing some of Chu's records, because the sidemen that he would pick, you loved to play with.
Yeah, a band like that I'm sure.
See you liked to play with guys like that, so that's one of the main things that is outstanding about the whole sessions, you just liked to play with those guys. They were all good players.
When you went with Cab you replaced Leroy Maxey who had been with him for a long time.
Been with him as long as I knew. There was a Cab Calloway.
Right. Why did he decide to leave?
I don't know. I think Leroy had been with Cab so long I guess he wanted to go back home to Kansas City, I know that's where I saw him. We played Kansas City.
Yeah, it says Leroy remained with Cab until November, 1938, when serious illness forced him to retire from full time music. Has lived for many years in Flint, Michigan.
I didn't know that was his home.
Apparently still alive as of this book which this edition is about a year old. So he's probably still alive.
Still alive probably. I haven't seen Leroy
since then, since we were in Kansas City.
Yeah, that was it for him, I guess. So did Chu get you on the band?
No, Walter Thomas got me on the band, Foots.
Tenor player.

Yeah, Foots Thomas is the one got me on the band. And I didn't want to join the band first because I was having a ball over there on 52nd Street with Stuff. Stuff Smith, small band, and of course, with Cab's band, Cab and Duke then were the highest paid bands out there, which was $100 a week, but see with Cab I was getting $150 and so was Chu. See we were featured members of the band so we made $150 apiece, but the top salary then was really $100 a week. Cab and Duke was the only ones that could afford to pay that. The rest of those bands, $75, $80, you know.
Did you get any expenses taken out in addition to the salary.

No, you paid your own expenses. Of course when you went on the road and you had those sleepers, you didn't have to pay for that. You had to pay for your lodging, I mean your board. But then but that was good money and steady work.
How many weeks out of the year did you work?
Oh damn near 52 about. 48. We worked all the time.
Did you get like a week off for Christmas or something like that?
Sometimes, maybe not, because we did a lot of benefits in those days. Time you look around you had a benefit to do.
What kind of benefits?

Well, PAL, different charities, Red Cross, oh goodness, just a lot of little different private little things we used to do. And that kept you quite busy. We were never off around the holidays, that seemed to be our busiest part. Busy season.
Well did Cab ever have a hit record?
Yeah he had "Hi Di Ho."
That was, I didn't know whether that was an expression....
And then "Jim Jam Jumpin'." You remember "Jim Jam Jumpin' with the jumpin' jive." That was a hit.
Because as you said he was one of the best paying band.
Oh yeah.
He certainly could afford to have the best playing band.
Oh yeah, yeah. He and Duke were the highest paid bands out there. And that was the going salary, $100 a week. Everybody jumped at that.
Plus it was a great band to play with.
Oh sure, you get the best places to work, just everything, oh yeah. Great band. But that was the
going price, Duke and Cab.
Let's talk about some of the people on there. We talked about Chu already and we kind of touched on Dizzy, but anything else stand out about Dizzy?

No, I know that when Dizzy joined the band, I really loved Dizzy's playing because then he played to me exactly like Roy Eldridge and I just loved the way Roy played and Dizzy sounded exactly like Roy to me with the exception of a few little things that Dizzy used to do. But I liked Dizzy's playing. Milt Henton, very good bass player, there's another boy in there by the name of Hilton Jefferson.
Lead alto player.
Yes. Very good. He made a recording there with Cab, 'Willow Weep for Me', Jimmy Dorsey.
Which is a great record.
Jimmy Dorsey was just crazy about it.
Did you know Hilton very well?
Oh yeah, yeah, very well.
He never went on to get the success something like Willie Smith.

No, no, he was a very quiet sort of a fellow, but very, I don't know, he had a subdued way about him, he never said much, you know, and very quiet, wasn't aggressive no kind of way you know, just very quiet, very nice. Everybody just loved Jeff, they called him, ongoing,
you know and just always quiet and could play that alto saxophone though.
He was a great player.
Yeah, yeah. Hilton Jefferson, then there was Jerry Blake, he was in that band.
Second alto. He was the clarinet soloist.
Yeah, him. Foots Thomas.
Apparently what Jerry Blake, let me just check this to make sure, but he ended up in a mental institution.
Is he? I haven't heard or seen of him since I left the band.
I think I--suffered mental breakdown and spent many years in a sanitorium where he died in 1961.
Oh he died, huh. I didn't know that. In 1961.
'61, right. Why don't we just run down--one thing about Dizzy is that Dizzy arranged "Paradiddle".
"Paradiddle," , mm hmm.
Let's talk about those things. There were three things that you did with that band that were features for you and one was "Paradiddle" and the other two were "Ratamacue" and "Crescendo on Drums"
And Dizzy made the arrangement on "Paradiddle". Walter Thomas made the arrangement on "Ratamacue."
And how about "Crescendo."
Walter made that arrangement for Cab's band.
"Ratamacue" is recorded with your first session with that band.
With Cab.
In 1939. How did that come about?

Well in between sets. See there at the Cotton Club, I used to go upstairs and practice on my practice pad. And we used to practice a lot of rudiments. In which the rudiments is drumming as ratamacue, paradiddle, Flam, Double stroke roll, Single stroke roll, etc. So I was upstairs practicing this ratamacue.
What precisely is a ratamacue?
A ratamacue, it's a beat, it's a drag, it's like ba da da da da, ba da da da da (DRUMMING).
And paradiddle is--
Okay.

Now a ratamacue has a little more meat to it than a paradiddle and so Walter Thomas was upstairs while I was practicing. And I called him, I said Foots, let's try to make an arrangement on this and call it "Ratamacue" and he sit up there and we did it. Got together with him, he's the one that got it. Now of course with RATAMACUE that beat is a little fast, I did it like this then (DRUMMING). But if it's fast (DRUMMING) . . . it's a bounce the way you do it with the sticks (DRUMMING) . . . And that's how "Ratamacue"
came about. Now "Crescendo in Drums"--
You mentioned you had done that with--
With Stuff and but Walter did a big band arrangement of it, but the same outline as what we had already done.
Let's see, Dizzy did the chart on "Paradiddle."
"Paradiddle" which was--
Did he do many charts for the band?
That's the only one I know Dizzy did.
Apparently he also did "Pickin' the Cabbage."
"Pickin' the Cabbage" I think was his, yeah, yeah.
Who did the arrangement of "Bye Bye Blues."
I think it was Tyree Glenn.
And speaking of Benny Carter, there are a couple of Benny's charts in the book. "Lonesome Nights." And "Calling all Bars."
"Calling All Bars," yeah.
That was a Leonard Feather tune that he arranged. Well anyway to get back to those features you did, what was the response you got from the audience, from the band?

Well the whole three of them, the biggest response came from "Paradiddle," the next was Crescendo, then "Ratamacue." But the biggest response was we used to use "Paradiddle" to close the show, all of Cab's shows when we would be on the road, we used to use that "Paradiddle" to
close the show, so we got the biggest response from that number. Sometimes we'd use "Crescendo on Drums", people would request it. So I'd say "Paradiddle" was the biggest thing, drum.
You were probably one of the first drummers besides Krupa to be really featured that much with a band, weren't you?
Yeah, I would say that, yes. And of course Johnny Morris, you remember that number he did, with Tony Pastor (HUMMING). I forget now, Johnny Morris, I think that was.
What kind of audience reception did you get?

Did I get? Very good, very good. With all of the drum numbers I'd say the biggest one was "Paradiddle." The next one was "Crescendo" and then the next one was "Ratamacue." "Ratamacue" got a nice hand, audience reception, and "Crescendo." But "Paradiddle" was the flag waver.
Let's see, let's talk about some of the other people who were in the band.
Danny Barker.
Danny Barker.
Guitar player. He's in New Orleans now.
Still very active.
Yeah, yeah, doing very good. We saw him on a couple of years ago, was all out to his home and had

gumbo and things, yeah, Danny's doing very well there, he's got a little group. He's over at some college teaching, too. Just forget what his schedule is over there. I know he's teaching in some college, and then he does quite a few of those concert dates around there, and then he's in and out of town quite a bit.
And of course there's Milt Hinton.
Oh Milt, he's just The Judge, he is the main stay of a lot of bands around in New York today, he's one of the great bass players that has played with everybody.
No question.
Yeah, all the bands and everybody would love to have Milt to come in there and play bass.

I recall reading a story about the first night he was on the band, where he was given a band uniform which was about ten sizes too big for him. And he had that solo that he had to do on 'Plucking the Bass.'
'Plucking the Bass,' yeah.
Do you remember that?
Yeah, yeah.
Do you remember that night?

Yeah, and Plucking that Bass and I think he wasn't too satisfied with it. And Benny Payne said 'well just stay right there and hit an F chord or something.' I just forget now, just how the conversation went down, but he was slapping that bass like Pops Foster.
Were you and Milt pretty close?

Oh yeah, yeah. Tell you what happened. Andy Kirk's band played the Howard Theatre in Washington and always when you play the Howard Theatre you play the Royal Theater the next week. Well the Royal Theatre was in Baltimore. The trip time from Washington to Baltimore is just an hour. So anyway when a band would close at the Howard Theatre that night, the next band come in the next day. Well the band that closed would always wait and see what this other band was going to play, because the first show at the Royal Theatre in Baltimore wasn't until about 3:00 where the shows at the Howard theatre the half-hour was 12:00, so therefore you went on at 12:30. So Andy Kirk's band had just closed. So Andy Kirk's band stood around; they wanted to see all the guys in Cab's band. So Ben Thigpen and I were good friends, all of them, Johnny Williams and all the boys, but anyway the drummers, you know, we stuck together. So Ben Thigpen and I sit down in the dressing room, was downstairs, and started drinking. Just a little sip, you know, just glad to see each other, telling stories, lying and going on, you know, so the bell rang for the half-hour. Okay, so you get up and start putting your uniform on. I hadn't stood up all the time that I was there drinking with Ben. I went to stand up I said, damn Ben, do you know I'm half high? I stood up there, was scuffling, trying to get
myself together, I said doggone, let me drink some coffee here and get myself together. So anyway, I did and got up on stage and all Andy Kirk's band was sitting, you know--are we still going?
Yes.

Sitting in the audience and so we closed with "Paradiddle". So Diz, Lamar Wright and Chad Collins was sitting right next to me. I was elevated and they're on that tier right next to me, and so "Paradiddle" came up there and that was upstairs, really fast. So I started it off and boy it was going great, fast, I had it a little faster than I really wanted to, but I made it. So it was on the cymbal for a while, tom-toms, snare drum things, so by then I was going so fast it sort of got me all messed up because I'm half high and I just couldn't get off that cymbal to get on the snare drum and tom-toms to get that coordination going, so Diz hollered over to me, "For Christ sake, get off that cymbal." I remember saying, "Diz, I can't, because if I do, I'll fall down." So anyway I managed to get off it and we got through, the curtain closed. Well Milt Hinton was on this side of me, he lays his bass down and I jump up and bam, step right in his bass, knock his sound post and all down, and I was so brought down, and Milt just looked at me and said, "Damn, Cozy," and boy, I felt like crying. But you know how you feel behind something like that. I says "Milt, I'll just buy you a new bass, just, I'm so drugged I'm brought down."

But luckily all I did was knock the sound post out and so he got somebody and they fixed the sound post and it was good, he could use his bass. But he'll tell you about that story right today. "Cozy, you remember that time you stepped in my bass?" I said "I never will forget it."
I'll bet.
Oh boy. Yeah, there were some great times in that band, Lamar Wright, was a great trumpet player.
Was he the lead player?
He was the high note player. You know, Pop Smith* was the lead man.
Yeah, okay. He was a great lead post.
Then Claude Jones was there, trombone; then Tyree and Keg Johnson.

Pop Smith I heard of a record he did with Fletcher Henderson around 1930 and he was hitting like a high up then. And you know Louie Armstrong was doing that like a clown act at the time. But had written into the arrangement. Pops was hitting it.
Yeah Pop Smith, he had two brothers, Luke and Joe, all of them were good trumpet players. Luke Smith and Joe Smith. All of them were with Fletcher Henderson, all of them great trumpet players.
Let's see, you mentioned of course Thomas.
Foots, yeah.
You mentioned Foots Thomas.
Foots, yeah. He arranged. He was a good arranger. He was a good section man. Played nice solos, mostly a good section man. He had been with Cab for years.
When Chu died who did they--
Teddy McRae. Teddy McRae came in after Chu.
Right. How did he do?
Did good. He wasn't a Chu Berry, but Teddy is a good saxophone player. Did very nice. Yeah, Teddy McRae.
I'm just going over some of the other people. Benny Payne is still with Billy Daniels now.
Yeah he's still with Benny, with Billy Daniels, yeah. He was with Cab for years. Billy Payne.
Let's see, who else do we have here? I see some of the people who wrote for that band, Don Redman.
Don Redman.
Did you know Don very well?
Oh yeah, yeah, very well.
Did you ever work with him outside that band?
I worked with Don on one of his recording dates. And that was all. But I knew Don very well. We used to play Hearts together. Yeah, Don. Very good arranger. Don Redman.
Buster Harding.
Buster Harding, yeah. Yeah, he was arranging then for Cab. Andy Gibson arranged for me.
And of course Edgar Battle.
Edgar Battle, yeah.
Who wrote 'Topsy'.
Oh yeah. /BK: You worked in quite a few bands with Edgar Battle.
Yeah. With Blanche Calloway, Willie Bryant.
There was Butter Jackson we've talked about.
(End of Side 'A')
Did you know him very well?
Quentin, oh yeah, yeah. Quentin very well. Quentin with Cab.
Was he doing the plunger things then?
The what?
The plunger thing.
No, because Cab, because Tyree was doing it.
Later when he was with Duke and Thad Jones and Mel Lewis he was doing the plunger.
The plunger things, yeah. See Tyree was doing the plunger things then.
Tyree was also a good vibes player.
Oh yeah, yeah.
Did you have much in the way of discussions with him about vibes or things like that?
Yeah, yeah, yeah with Tyree. Tyree and I were really tight, you know, we used to sit down and talk

and of course play together. I've used him on some of my recordings. And we were very close. Had a lot of nice discussions regarding music you know and been out to his home and his wife Gloria and sit down and eat and talk.
I guess his sons--
Yeah very good. One of them plays--
Roger. ...flute and vibes.
Yeah, Roger very good.
I heard him at Mongo Santa Maria a few years ago. Then of course there's Jonah.
Jonah, oh yeah, well Jonah you know about him. Yeah, Jonah.
What about Cab himself?

Cab, well, Cab mostly was an entertainer. And he studied music. I think he studied saxophone with Walter, Foots and some of them, but I guess a man the caliber that Cab was, I mean, couldn't devote too much time to studying music at that part of the game, you know, he was a big top man now you know, what's he going to study saxophone for. He studied it enough you know, and that stage of the game you know I guess he would have been able to be, if he continued, a good saxophone player.
In the way that Billy Eckstein was a decent trumpet player, trombone player.
Yeah, you see that stage of the game they've already made it, they're stars already. Now you've got to

set them down and let them start taking the instruments, starting back there with the ABCs, you know that ain't going to make it too much, you know, and Cab was good. I learned a lot. Cab was very disciplined, his band was.
I remember, Panama Francis took your place, right, eventually?
J. C. Heard took my place, then Panama took J.C.'s.
Because I've looked over Panama's oral history interview and he said that I guess as you said, Cab was very disciplined and he insisted on the band being punctual and sober ...

Like, you know, how they used to have cliques in bands, Cab says I'll fire the clique. You know, he never stood for any foolishness, which was good, very good discipline, nobody, everybody was there on time. You know paying that kind of money you know, and he was very good, he wouldn't repimand anybody unless they caused him to do so. He was very strict.

I think Panama mentioned that there was, or maybe it was Milt Hinton mentioned that there was a ritual about if you got a certain color check that meant that you were still on the band, but if you got like a pink check, that meant that you got your two weeks' notice, something like that.
Well I didn't experience that while I was in the band, maybe that happened later when Panama was in there. But Cab, oh he was just great, great to work for.
So you stayed, let's see ... you made a lot of records with him.
I was with Cab from '39 through '43, wasn't it, '42?
'42. According to this. But you did a tremendous number of records there.
Oh yeah.
What's your favorite recording from that band, do you have one?
From Cab's band?
Yeah.

Of course the drum, I like "Paradiddle" better than Crescendo and "Ratamacue". The other ones we had, Ensemble things, I don't know which one to pick. "Pickin' Cabbage" was good. I've got to listen to them altogether really and pick them out again, I forget just the whole texture or the whole thing of the tunes, but "Pickin' Cabbage" was good, I liked that. "Willow Weep for Me" was good, "Ghost of a Chance" was good.
With Chu Berry, yeah.
Yeah, with Chu Berry. All those things were very good.
That was your last time that you really
spent regularly with the band, right, as far as a road band.
With Cab?
Yeah. You did other big bands later, but they weren't road bands, right?
Yeah, Benny Goodman.
Did you go on the road with him?
I went to Philly with him.
I know you did Seven Lively Arts with him.

No, I took the band in Seven Lively Arts. See, there's the thing. Billy Rose produced Carmen Jones and Seven Lively Arts. See Carmen Jones was at the Broadway Theatre right there at 53rd and Broadway, where Seven Lively Arts was at 52nd and Sixth Avenue, 51st and 6th Avenue. So Billy Rose produced both of them. So Benny Goodman had the band at Seven Lively Arts, which the stars were Bea Lillie, Burt Lahr and Benny Goodman. So Benny had the band, five pieces.
Oh that's all it was. I thought it was a big band.

No small group, because it was, little scene where Billy Rose sold the Metropolitan Opera House and Benny Goodman had his five pieces or six, I just forget what it was, Red Norvo was in there and all these showgirls were around him. It was a beautiful scene. Well when Benny Goodman cut out, see the show wasn't a great hit but it

ran for a little while, so Benny Goodman got the best of it. About first six or eight weeks, months of it. So there were another four, five months of it to go, but Benny cut out because he had other commitments to do. So Billy Rose was around auditioning bands, but he couldn't find a band that could, that he liked. So he says, Cozy, come on get five pieces together and come on and replace Benny. I've been auditioning bands, and I don't have a band yet. So I wasn't worried about it too much because he's the producer of both shows and whatever he says goes. I mean if he wants me in that show, good. He knows the part that I'm playing, in the Broadway show, Carmen Jones, because I was in the pit with Carmen Jones, and then I did a thing on stage with 'the Gypsy Song.' Beat out the rhythm on the drum with the girls dancing up there, so after that, I did that and that closed the intermission. Well see right after intermission is when the Benny Goodman thing went on at the Zeigfield Theatre. Well all I had to do was just change my tuxedo on and go over there and put this spangle little black jacket on with sequins on it and go out there and do that little, all it was was five minutes. 'All we played was 'Stompin' at the Savoy' and 'Hallelujah.' Two numbers. And...
How far apart were the two theaters?
53rd and Broadway and 51st and Sixth Avenue, took me about five minutes to walk over there, altogether it

was about 20 minutes, I could get over there, get in the uniform, do the two numbers and back. And so there, see, I was doing two Broadway shows at the same time. Two Broadway shows, and they were good shows because my name was on the playbill of each, see, and so I did two Broadway shows right at the same time and that's, I'm the one that replaced Benny. I did that for about four months and what I did I got men right off 52nd Street who were working on 52nd Street to do it, because all they had to do was come over there during their intermission, 52nd and Sixth Avenue, the theatre was right at 51st and 6th Avenue, so I got Don Byas, Billy Taylor piano, Tiny Grimes.
How about a bass player.
Billy Taylor Sr., bass. He's in Washington now and me.
Who was the piano player?
Billy Taylor.
Oh the other Billy Taylor.
And Don Byas, Tiny Grimes.
Did you know Don Byas very well?
Oh God yeah, I just saw him before he died.
Sure.
You mean when he was back in this country.
Oh yeah.
Where did you see him?
In New York and saw him in Chicago. I was
one of the first ones he called when he was there making some records with, what the devil is his name, for Dan Morgan.....
There was TV show that I saw, you know he sounded good. A friend of mine heard him around that time, but he didn't sound so good. How did he sound to you?
He sounded good to me that day, he wasn't drinking, you know.
Yeah, he sounded great on the TV show.
Don Byas.
He started to drink again?
Yeah.
By the time you saw him. Because I guess when he was in Europe he was just totally on the wagon.
Yeah, he was really ... he was doing scuba diving and all that, he was doing great, got back over here and started drinking. It's too bad.
Temperamentally he was a pretty aggressive guy, right?
Yeah, yeah, oh goodness he's been on so many recordings of mine. One of them was one of Foots Thomas' originals 'Buy Us a Drink.' Don Byas, great tenor player.
No question, yeah.
Got a picture of him, Don Byas, Coleman Hawkins and Thelonious Monk.
From 52nd Street, huh?
Yeah, it's right there hanging in my archives.

I'll have to look at that. We were just looking at some more pictures from Cozy's archives, and one of the photos he showed me was one from 52nd Street with Coleman Hawkins, Don Bias, Benny Harris, Thelonious Monk, Al Hall and himself. That's a pretty famous photo. I've seen that in books.
Oh you have?
Yeah, several of them.
At one time there, Don Bias and Coleman Hawkins had a regular little act that they were doing together, they worked on 52nd Street as a duo for weeks at a time.
I didn't know that.
Oh yeah, yeah. Don and Hawk. It was a good combination, both of them. The same way with Lockjaws and Jimmy.
Johnny Griffin.
Johnny Griffin. They worked in the Metropole as a duo together for weeks, yeah, Johnny Griffin and Lockjaws.
With a regular rhythm section?
Yeah, they had a regular rhythm section.
And you were working opposite them?
Yes, I had my band in there then. Or was I with Red Allen? It may have been with Red Allen I don't know. One time I was with Red and then one time they were still there and I had my own group.
I see. We didn't talk about Hawkins at all. Did you know him very well?

Oh boy, that was my man, Coleman Hawkins. Oh God, I can't say anything that hasn't already been said about Hawk. I made a lot of records with him, and sit around, been to his apartment so many times and sit down and talked and been around to different little joints with him. We'd go into. And just so many different things. Ride uptown together. Kirby, Hawk and I, we all used to sit around and discuss automobiles. They both liked the Chrysler and they were the ones made me buy a Chrysler at the time because I was a Cadillac man then, you know. They said oh Cozy, this Chrysler. They made me get a Chrysler and I liked it. He and Kirby loved the Chrysler. Do you remember the DeSalle?
Yeah.
That was another good car. Kirby and Hawk had, and I had one too. Yeah, a DeSalle, yeah that was it.
Did you see Hawk very often during the last years....

No I didn't. I didn't see Hawk all the time that he was growing a beard. I didn't see the Hawk. I know that one time we were all by to see Shorty Baker, he was at the Alvin Hotel and we all stopped by to see him, he wasn't feeling too well.
With Duke?
Yeah with Duke. And Horace....
Horace Henderson?
No, Horace Silver, not Horace Silver.
Horace Henderson?

No. A trumpet player. Anyway he came by, he says 'Hot doggit, it you know who I just saw? Hawk out there on Broadway, looked just like Jesus.' Well I hadn't seen Hawk. See, and then, Evelyn hadn't seen Hawk really perform, see, because I been knowing Hawk way back there before I even started, you see I knew Hawk way before he knew me. And Hawk always used to dress immaculate and keep that horn immaculate, man, just as clean, at the time. There was a store there, Laytons and Phil Kronfield, where you used to go buy men's clothes, Hawk used to go there then, way back there then to buy hundred-dollar suits, two hundred-dollar suits, tuxedos, man, he was a beautiful dresser. So he came here to Columbus and I wrote to Evelyn and said, please go by and see Coleman Hawkins because he's a great tenor player, which he was, and she went by and she says, 'Cozy, I know that you may not like this but he just looked terrible. He had this beard, it wasn't combed, his suit wasn't pressed, like cigarette ashes all over his tuxedo, and they had to help him up on the bandstand, and he said it was just terrible.'
Well he was drinking himself to death.
Yep, and said he could hardly play. I said oh, that's too bad. So that was her thoughts of Coleman Hawkins, the only time she heard him. But see I knew better

than that at the time that Hawk was well, you know, but he just drank himself to death. Drank himself to death, it was too bad. I don't know for what reason. You never know what's on anybody's mind that does something like that. They say he just went down to nothing. And with that beard growing, he wouldn't comb it (TOO LOW) ... Roy Eldridge told me about him. He said 'Cozy, you wouldn't want to see Hawk, knowing Hawk in the earlier years.' He was a fashion plate.
Oh yeah, he had expensive tastes and everything.
Oh boy, all the tenor players loved him. All the tenor players used to almost cry when they'd hear Hawk play the last year or so that they were out there. Because he wasn't playing anything.
You mentioned Roy Eldridge. Let's talk about him for a while.

Roy, we made all his records with Billie Holiday together. Roy, Benny Goodman, Ben, Teddy Wilson, Kirby. We made the first records, 'Miss Brown to You,' 'What a Little Moonlight Can Do.' Roy was on those. Then I made so many records with Roy, 'Braggin' In Brass,' all those things. Roy, Charlie Shavers, Joe Thomas.
Joe Thomas the tenor player?

No, the trumpet player, the trumpet player. Yeah, Roy, he, great musician, great stylist. He set the pace for many a trumpet player out here. Roy Eldridge did. Roy and Charlie Shavers. I knew Bunny Berigan real good.

Oh yeah. Well.

Yes, they are. Well, from working together. See this Ernie Bullock, clarinet player, he was very good, of course his technique just fit what Jelly Roll was doing, and the men surrounded by him, you know, they knew just what riff he was going to play or in which direction he was going to lead them.

No.

The big band and the what you mean the ad lib groups or the small groups or....
Yeah.
Or, I guess the ad lib groups, when you're saying the big band, well--
Big band as opposed to a small group.

Well a big band is mostly if you have charts to play, you've got to stick to the chart as close as you can. Of course, little things, I mean you've got to ad lib on you know, you just can't play a chart exactly as it's written. It's just like Duke said, after an arrangement is a thing there that is, notes that will guide everybody in the right direction. Now after you learn, or after you play the notes, everybody gets acquainted with the notes, your da! segno signs, the structure, the whole arrangement, now after everybody plays their arrangement down, now the thing to do is let's put some character to that arrangement, bend
the note here, bend the note there. See...

No, that's right, and well so Sonny knew backwards and Louie Bellson too, you know, and then the charts. Now you've got to adapt yourself to, first you should know what a big band should sound like, a drummer when he sits in with a big band, first thing he's got to figure is what can he do to enhance that arrangement that this big band is doing. Now he can stick to his charts, he can have his drum chart written out there, but a lot of little things he can do, little kick beats that he can do that will enhance the whole band, and anybody see, any well schooled musician can sit down and play note after note, but it'll sound very stiff if that's all you're doing is just playing what's written on that paper, note after note, sometimes it'll sound good, if it's a saxophone chorus and the saxophones are all breathing together and you take the breath at the same time or brass or whatever. And that will sound good, but everybody just to sit up there and just play those notes as they're written. Say like if you have four quarter notes .... all right now maybe in that arrangement you can bend those notes a little bit ... and sort of bend them a little, put little slurs over them.

That's the thing that I'm talking about, you've got to add character to them. Now, with a small group, the way I do, you sit down and you start playing with a small group and then you listen. That's a little tour I took with them, just me myself, it was an all-star group. It was Jack Teagarden, Earl Hines were heading the group, was Peanuts Hucko; Max Kaminsky; Jack Lesberg and me. We did about 18 days over in Europe, but it was headed by Jack Teagarden and Earl Hines.
I assume it went over very well.
Oh yeah. That was a good group.
You did a record that I want to talk a little about because that was kind of an interesting record.
The Cozy Conception of Carmen.
Carmen, okay.
That came out in '61.
Yeah.
I imagine that was kind of an outgrowth of Carmen Jones.
That's right.
Whose idea was it to do that record?

Mine. And I loved all of those arias from the opera Carmen, and I just did it my way and put a little beat behind a lot of them you know, and start swinging those arias. Now I never tried to distort the melody, because there's too many opera lovers out there that love the melody of 'Carmen', so you can't go and tear that melody apart. But I did stick to the melody only I added a little more rhythm.
Let's see for the record, for the personnel on it, that was--
That was a big band, that was 19, 20 pieces.
That much?
Way. Dick Hyman made the arrangements.
Oh he did the charts.
Yup and a boy named Bob Hammer.
Who later did arranging for Mingus' band.
Yeah, yeah.
It's listed here as George Holt and Bernie
Privin on trumpets, Jerome Richardson on clarinet, baritone, Al Klink and John Hafer on, it's listed as tenor sax, but I hear on the record a lot of flute and piccolo. Which I'm sure they play also.
Yeah yea, Jerome Richardson.
Yeah, Jerome's a very good flute player.
Yeah.
And Bob Hammer on piano, either Milt Hinton or Jack Lesberg on bass.
Milt Krauss on drums.
Doug Allen.
Yeah it was a big band.
On percussion. Yeah. And that was for Charlie Parker Records.
That's right, at the time.
That ended up somehow on the Everest label we were talking about.
I think after Charlie Parker wasn't it MGM.
It has Summit here, which is probably an MGM.
MGM thing.
Subsidiary, yeah. But it's interesting. Some of the writing on there that Dick did reminds me a little bit of the Sauter-Finnegan band.
Yeah, yeah.
With all the flute and piccolos. With the
Mallet percussion. Did some very nice writing.
Oh yeah, very nice.
And you also did a record with Henry Jerome and yourself and three other drummers.

Yeah, they were my guests on this album, It was Henry Jerome's idea and we did all commercial tunes, and each of us had a track. It was my guest on the albums were Gene Krupa, Ray McKinley and Panama Francis.
And that was done in '62 for Coral.
Coral, that's right.

And you also did another record for Coral with Henry Jerome, well a couple of those tracks you redid 'Topsy' and you did 'Big Noise from Winnetka', they were on that cassette that I gave you last night. And that's the last thing that's listed in your discography in the early '60s. Let me just look over for a second. You had been recording under your own name since the early '40s with very small groups.
My first record date ever was with under my name was with Harry Lim. He is the one that sponsored it.

Curiously, that's not listed. The first one listed in Jeffson, it's under the Cozy Cole All Stars in February of '44 with Joe Thomas the trumpeter, Tommy Young, Coleman Hawkins, Earl Hines, Teddy Walters and Billy Taylor.
That's the same date, I think.
Oh the same date.
Yeah.
Then Ray Lim was the producer.
Yeah, Harry.

Oh, Harry Lim, excuse me. From then on you were recording pretty regularly for the Savoy label, Continental label, Keynote, the old--and some of the others that we already talked about. Well, let's see. According to Chilton, led own group at the Metropole during early '60s." So you kept that up and said you toured Africa with your own quintet in the Autumn of '62 to early 1963. You've got a picture up on your wall from that.

That's right, with the whole show. See now that whole show consisted of my band, which was six pieces, five pieces, trumpet, tenor and three rhythm. And I had other acts with me which all my band was black in the band and then I had six white acts. See we were commissioned through the State Department out of New York and we toured Africa for five months and was accepted very well. And we ran about 15 countries and 85 cities and that's another one of the highlights of my career. It was very hot over there in Africa, but after all, everybody was over there for a while, we got used to it. But we started off in North Africa around Casablanca, Oran, Algiers, then we went down into Black Africa, starting at Dakar, Senegal,

Sierre Leone, Monrovia, Liberia, Nigeria, Abidjian, Guinea, May 14, anyway it was about 15 countries, all up in the Cameroons, up around Duala. That's up near the Equator. But mostly it was West Africa and Equatorial Africa that we visited and played, did concerts.
What kind of a reception did you get?

Oh just great. Well drums is a language over there, you know, and so you had it halfway made then. But I had an actor with me that blew up balloons, Barney and John Shirley. He could make different balloons, all different kind of animals. They were just terrific. Then I had a singing act, I had a Mistress of Ceremonies with me by the name of Mildred Clinton. She used to go with me on these interviews. She spoke French fluently, and she was a great help. Then I had a family of three, the Riches. He played drums and little the son did, and the Riches sang and danced and played the xylophones. But it was entertaining little show, it got some very nice write ups. I have so many of the writeups and all of the pictures, and just everything, almost a suitcase full of it from that African tour.
So I guess the reception must have been very good.

Oh yeah, yeah, it was. Well, see you almost had it made when you go over there with drums. If you can just keep a little rhythm and play a lot of tom-toms. Then after we got there, see, we picked up on some of that
high-life music, then my bass player, Ivan Rolle, he could dance that dance, highlife dance and that broke it up really.
Is that pretty close to raggae?
I think so, yeah, the highlife?
Yeah.
Yeah, it's nothing to do, you just walk and (HUMMING) ... it's just. You're just walking.
Probably in that heat you can't do much more strenuous than that.
No, no and just walk, you know and you just go on and do it.
So that lasted for a few months.
Five months. Five months.
It said you were regularly featured on television shows.
Yes.
You mentioned a few of those.
Well.
Anything else in that vein?
No. Let's see, well the Johnny Carson Show and what's that other show that comes on in the morning at 1:30?
That's on now or used to be?
It used to be. 1:30 in New York used to come on. Joe Franklin. Joe Franklin. Memory Lane, was that it?
He calls it the Joe Franklin show.
Yeah, I guess that's it, it's not Memory Lane, I got it mixed up with another show. Yeah, Joe Franklin. He's still on, isn't he?

As far as I know, yeah. It's a local show that's been going for years. It says that you appeared in several films. We talked about Make Mine Music, and you were in The Glenn Miller Story with Jimmy Stewart and June Allison. How did they work in that one?
Yeah. Louie, the whole band.
That's right, I forgot about that.

Yeah Louie's band was in it, so that included me in there with the band. Then Gene Krupa and I did a little thing in there together, drum thing. Then I did The Strip with Mickey Rooney, which I wasn't photographed in it, I did the soundtrack and Mickey Rooney did the synching of it, synchronizing.
What was that about?

The Strip? It's one of those love scenes with Mickey and what was the gal's name, he had a leading lady, she was just a starlet at the time. Thought it was a good little picture, didn't last too long. Didn't last too long, but it was nice making it, you know.
And in the late '60s you went back with Jonah.
With his small group, his quintet. How long did you stay with him?
Up until just here a couple of years ago, just left him, which was, what is this '80? About '77.
Is he working much these days?
Not too much. I know he's going to do that Grand Prix in Morocco. May the 10th, I just talked to the bass player a couple of weeks ago.
Who's his bass player now?
My bass player, Ivan Rollé. And...
You two must be very close.

Oh yeah, Jonah and I, way we're doing close way back there with Stuff. Billie Holiday back there, Cab. On up through the years. Then of course I first met Jonah hearing Stuff. I first went to Buffalo, in 1934, '33, around there. See, so Jonah and I are real way back buddies, way back.
He's kind of an underrated player.
Yeah, Jonah always could play. The same way he's playing now.
He's a good lead--was he a lead trumpet player at all?
With Cab, no. See, the lead trumpet player with Cab was a boy by the name of Doc Cheatham.
That's right, Doc was a lead player a long time (CROSS TALK)
A long time. Jonah was third trumpet with Dizzy and mostly had all the solos, Chad Collins. Jonah didn't play too much with Cab, he wasn't featured too much, maybe on one or two numbers.
But he sounds like he could be a good lead player, he's got the conception for it and the range.
And the power, yeah. He's a good trumpet player.
No question.
Yeah, Jonah's a very good trumpet player.
Let's talk about what you've been doing these days. You said you had been living in Columbus for about 17 years.

Yeah, about 17 years, Bill, and I've become very acquainted with the town and I like it very much. And of course this would be my senior year at Capital University, it's very relaxing here, it's a nice town, you know, just, it isn't that knock-down, drag-out, bam bam bam, like New York, you know. I remember when I first came here, Bill, it was hard for me to get used to it, because I'd be jay-walking and things like that you know, in New York, you're just high strung, you're liable to cross the street if you just see a little opening because things are moving so fast. Well I was doing the same thing here, a lot of times I used to come here, or any time that I would leave New York, you know, you say oh goodness, when you leave New York you're camping out. Let me get back to the Apple. But now, I don't think that I would be able to live in New York again and feel real good, at my age now. Because it's too much

of a scuffle there now. I was wondering how I made it as long as I did, but I was much younger and it was, I was there all the time, and I was used to it, and all my friends were there, But since I've been here, I've accumulated some very nice people, nice friends, and just enjoy it very much here.
What made you decide to move here?

Well I met my young lady here, Evelyn, and of course so many other different things, I like the town. See I been coming back and forth here the past 30 years with different bands, Cab, Louie, with my own group, I played here so many times in different places around here, Benny Klein's, Tommy Hendricks, the Roarin' Twenties Club around here, I've been playing in and out of Columbus for the past 30 years. So I have very nice tie-in with a lot of friends and club owners and everything around here. I wasn't new, it wasn't a new adventure, I already knew quite a bit about Columbus before I even came here to stay.
Okay, how long have you been going to Capital University?
Well this is my senior year this time, this year, 1980, so that has been 1976 was my freshman year.
So you're pretty close to a degree, huh?

Yeah, yeah. Well see my sickness, I had to fall out this last semester, so I have another year to go. But right now, I got my honorary degree, doctor's degree last year. Doctor of Musical Arts from Capital.
And this year, pardon me, they're doing two and a half hours of all the films that I had did up through the years and the contributions and all are going to a scholarship fund.
I read about that in Downbeat. Tell me more about that.

Well I thought it was a good idea, because Capital has been very good to me. All the faculty, the deans, and the president, just everybody, and I've enjoyed it. It's a very good music school and intimate it is, and it's a good school of learning, and I suggested this idea of doing, running these pictures for about two and a half hours, and we presented it to the president here, and he just loved the idea, and so that's what they're going to do.
And John Baker's supplying the film.
That's right, mmm hmmm. And so....
That'll be in a couple of weeks.
Yeah, the 27th is when it's showing, just before the semester closes.
The 27th of April. Yeah, that sounds great.
Yeah, I'm very pleased with it, looking forward to it.
What other movies can you recall, besides the ones we talked about, besides Make Mine Music and the Miller Story, and The Strip?
Well there was a couple I did there with Cab, short things.
Ten minute things.
Yeah. Then there was a couple I did there with Coleman Hawkins and Roy, just five minute things, ten minute things.
So you did some things with Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge.

Roy. And a lot of things I did back there, them that they are going to show, I almost forgot about them when I saw them in John Baker's home. I looked and I said when the hell did I do that? And it was way back there that I had forgotten about them, because they were just short little movies, you know, short little shots, but very effective at the time, and they say it was very good.
I'm sure it'll be a lot of fun.
Very exciting, they say, the two hours is.
I wish I could see it.
Yeah, I wish so too.
Well let's see, you mentioned that you had been still travelling on the road a good deal. What kind of work did you do during the '70s? Besides Jonah?
Besides Jonah, all these things with Barry Martin.
Yeah, let's talk about that, we didn't get that on the tape at all.
With Barry Martyn.
Who is a drummer in England.

Yes, yes, and then he's sponsoring, he is the manager and promoter of these European tours. And I did a couple of those since I been away from Jonah. And different things on my own, up in Canada I did a little skit up there about five or six days, concerts on my own, where there's a band right there. And I just work with them and sit in, I mean I just sit in with the local band.
Where in Canada?

Oh up around Vancouver, up in Calgary, Winnipeg, Montreal, Toronto. And of course Los Angeles. So I've been doing quite a bit of just free lancing concerts on my own. And I just did one up in--say, Evalene, where did I do that gig in, upstate? Grosse Pointe, Ann Arbor, Michigan.
Oh, up at the university?
A club there. Some fellow...gets groups and brings in individual artists.
Thank you.
So you have been working more and more lately with pickup groups.

Oh yeah, yeah, and I prefer it like that now, you know. It's no great big axe to grind, and just go on and have fun. You work with these good groups, you know, especially a good little organized group, they've got all their thing together. Very easy for me to sit in with them, you know.
So in other words, you go in and play their music.
Oh sure. And then I bring a couple of little charts maybe on 'Topsy' lead sheets, you know, a small group, all they need is a little trumpet, lead sheet, piano.
That poster you have up on your wall from last year in LA that you did, Barney Bigard and Trummy Young. Talk a little about that.
Oh surely. Well that was my first time seeing Trummy since, I mean working with Trummy since I left Louie.
He moved to Honolulu.

He moved to Honolulu, and he's doing very good out there, he's got a little band; he's working for the Hilton Hotels out there. Been there for year. This year they're going to do another trip for Barry Martyn, May 1st, which I had to cancel out because it was too near me coming out of the hospital, but that was a great little tour there with Trummy, Barney Bigard, Red Calendar bass player, and what the devil is his name, Duke Burrell on piano. And we just had a ball, it was very nice, and that was my second time, second year with them. Now the first year it wasn't Trummy Young, we had, instead of Trummy was Barney, Red Calendar, oh Benny Carter. Benny Carter, that's right. Let's see, who else can I think of. So I did two of those tours with .... Dick Carey was on one too. Art Hodges.
Who is still quite active.
Yes. He's still in Chicago, isn't he, Art Hodges?
Yeah, as a matter of fact, he works near Washington at a place called the King of France Tavern in Annapolis about a couple of times a year with Kenny Devern and Don Michael.
Oh I see.
So he's still travelling. I guess pretty active. You said you don't do too much local work here in Columbus because the money is generally not good.
No, the scale is all right, you know, but the money isn't that great, you know.

Do you do anything with--well obviously you said you were conducting, you had conducting classes that you were taking with the Capital University concert band. Do you do any playing with jazz bands there?

Oh yeah, I do several little clinics, several little seminars with the jazz arts group. Then with the small group and of course the jazz arts group is the big band, and the fusion band. I did a couple of little things there with them, you know.
... a fusion style ...
Good, good, you know, all of it's good music if the charts are good, you know, and, especially during I've sit on a lot of their recitals, you know, the junior

recitals, senior recitals, sit in with them, you know, which is a very big kick to me. And I stay busy over there doing that a lot of times. Doing those little recitals, seminars, clinics. I enjoy that.
And we talked yesterday about Benny Carter having come in not so long ago to do a concert.

Benny Carter, backed him, then Clark Terry was in just last month, but of course I was sick at the time. And the time that he was here before which was a year ago, I didn't play with him then because he had his own charts and he did it with the jazz arts group, but Clark has been here twice. Then Phil Woods, I worked with him, Phil Woods, I worked with him and did a little seminar with him there in the school. Yeah, Louie Bellson was here last year.
You said that you had written a chart that he's interested in recording.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
What's that like?
Well it's just a blues chart, blues chart. It's swinging, you know just one of those old gut bucket things and Louie likes it.
Great. What's the name of it?
'Ev.' Named after my wife. E V.
That's great.
Just a little old simple thing that's swinging, you know, not too many notes but nice riffs.
Have you sent that to him yet?
Not as yet, I haven't copied it off. As I told you I had the score-transposed score, I've got to get it off now on paper, and I've got to get that all set, you know set up and send it to him.
Well that'll be something to look forward to.

Oh yeah, yeah. I like the idea of that and then Louie, see, I remember when Louie won the Gene Krupa contest in drumming. I was with Benny Goodman right there at the Paramount Theatre, and he was right up the street at Wurlitzer's there on 42nd Street, and that's where they held it and that's where he won it.
So you've been all in all keeping quite active.
Yeah, quite busy.
You don't have a set of drums in the apartment, do you?
Yeah, a practice set, yeah.
I didn't see it. Can you practice here? Do the neighbors hassle you at all?
(Break in discussion)
Oh yeah..... I think we've got a nice little session going for the two days, don't you?
I think so, yeah. We were just looking at Cozy's rogue gallery.
Oh thank you.
Which is pretty impressive, which has photos going all the way back to his childhood and going through his days with Wilbur Sweatman and on and on and on.
Thank you.

And he was also showing me his practice setup which he's got kind of, it's a trap set up with a set of practice pads and cymbals that are carefully taped up and enable him to practice to his heart's content.
That's right.
Much to the envy of a horn player like myself who has to contend with neighbors all the time.

Yes, I know. But that's one reason why I like this apartment I have, as you see it's on the ground floor, it doesn't bother with anybody and I've got my little tapes and my little record players, my little earphones in there and I can just get in there and get my chops up good and wail until I fall out. And that's what I enjoy and it's my life and I'm so happy that I can do it, and I have a place such as this where I can practice like this and not annoy anyone.
Sure, it's an ideal setup.
Yes, it is.

Let's just maybe deal a little bit with let's say music that's come about in the last 20 years, such as rock and some of the more recent drummers, say somebody like Elvin Jones or people who have come around after him.
developments
What do you think about ... like that?

Well as far as the music is concerned, I've always said there is some good rock and there's some bad rock. The same way when the swing or the be-bop era was in, there was some good be-bop and there was some bad and that goes the same way with the music. Now as far as these drummers are concerned, there's Elvin Jones has got a very nice name, he happens to be one of the good ones. Some drummers that try to play like Elvin is very bad, they sound bad. And I would say that it runs in cycles like that. If you're good, you can play 'Home Sweet Home' so it sounds good. Sometimes you may be able to play Home Sweet Home and it'll sound bad, and drummers that try to play like Buddy Rich all of a sudden. Well they forget that Buddy Rich came up in that old school way back there with Joe Marsala, Artie Shaw, and they forget about Elvin Jones way back there with these other little bands. I think he was with, oh goodness, a lot of them little swing bands before he even started playing this.
Alvin used to play, I guess....
Jay McShann....
Sweets Edison.
Sweets Edison, and yeah, see, so he's got all that background in back of him. See so many guys try to — trumpet players try to play like Diz. Well Diz was way back

there with Fletcher Henderson, Jay McShann, Billy Eckstein, Cab Calloway. He's got all that footage underneath him. You know that kind of background. So Dizzy knows where it's at. A lot of these kids will try to start where Dizzy's at now and they don't know where it's at.
They get a few cliches under their fingers, but they really don't know what he's doing... or for that matter sax players who try to play like Coltrane.

Impossible, see 'cause Coltrane came up in that school, you know, good foundation, working with those bands, different bands, different style bands, and they try to pick up right where Coltrane is now before he died, or the same way with the drummers, try to play like Max or Roy Haynes or Elvin or Buddy, and you just can't you know, it's impossible to be made a doctor over night. There's no way in the world that I've said it over and over, that you can skip grade school and go to high school. See, you've got to pay those dues first, and find out where it's at and then from there on you can build and just build.
Do the students that you go to Capital with, is this basically what you tell them?

Yes, it's on that, that's the principle of it and you tell them that, of course some of them are very open minded and they appreciate the things. A lot of these young kids, they don't like a lot of these modern drummers, you know, they'll go way back and get some of Gene Krupa's

albums, Ray McKinley, Ray Baudac, go back and get some of those things, Jo Jones, they like that style. A lot of those young drummers don't like a Max Roach or Elvin Jones or like that you know. Some of them do, you know, but a lot of them don't.

There seems to have been a revival in the past few years. A lot of the players who came up, you know, before bebop and who were kind of neglected for a number of years, like Arnett Cobb. Is working a lot again.
Tenor player. Very good tenor player. Used to be with Hamp.
Right yeah. And he's working a lot again and Panama Francis has that revival of the Savoy Sultans is working a lot. George Kelly as a matter of fact.
Yeah George Kelly, they're all hometown boys. Out of Florida ... So is Al Cooper. He's out of Florida, the one who originated the Savoy Sultan. Al Cooper and the Savoy Sultans.
We can't end this interview without talking a little bit about your friend Edgar Battle. We mentioned him in passing a number of times but we never really delved.

Well Edgar Battle is, I finished telling you a little while ago that he was a very dear friend. Edgar Battle I've been knowing him, he is the one that recruited me out of New York to go with Blanche Calloway.
He was with Blanche and he says, Cozy, would you like to join Blanche Calloway, which was really my first band that I stayed with and got experience.
And didn't get nervous.

That's right. So Battle is the one that hired me for that job, and I imagine that Blanche at the time wanted to fire me one million times because I didn't know what segue meant. And you know the del segno signs and all that. And I had never played a show and Battles was very boisterous. You fire him, I'm the one that hired him, fire me too. So constant going on, couple, three months from there, playing shows and things like that is when I started to learn how to play shows. And from then on, you know, I was in the know. I mean I knew how to play shows, I knew how to segue and I got used to playing with the big bands. So, we were together, Battles and I worked together for a few years, then we both quit. Blanche was always on us about where'd Battles would always be telling, well you know, if you don't want to work for me I'll get the boy round the corner. And so as long as you can get musicians a dime a dozen here, you know. So anyway we used to sit in back of the bus and Battles and I quit Blanche Calloway at the same time. And it was down in Nashville, Tennessee, and we just took a Greyhound bus, put my drums there, then they had the carrier up on top of the buses then, the Greyhound buses, and came

to New York, and then's when I joined Benny Carter, and then later on after Benny Carter, I went with Willy Bryant and Battles was in that band with Willy Bryant. So in the meantime, during all that time, I've been seeing Battles, knowing him, and believe it or not, when I got this number together, 'Topsy', and mentioned it, and we had recorded, I didn't know Battles was the composer.
Amazing.
Isn't that something. I found out afterwards Battles was the composer.
He and Eddie Durham.

Eddie Durham, that's right. And that's how tight Battles and I was for years, and we were together with Willy Bryant as I told you and on just so many things, you know, we were just really hand in hand with him. Just before he died, he had a whole brochure and was about to put on, had a lot of people Singer Sewing Machine people interested in, a woman in authority with Columbia Broadcasting, she was interested in this show that he had written, the music and all of the dialogue and everything.
What was the name of the show?

The name of the show was Mr. Tom, and it was a regular, it was built around Uncle Tom's Cabin, and he says Cozy, a lot of people just thought that Uncle Tom was a regular Uncle Tom. He was a humanitarian. And it was

the truth that what he had in all the dialogue, these people were really interested in it, and it was going to be a big Broadway production, I imagine it would have been by now if he had lived. But the interest was lost after he left, and he wrote the music and all the lyrics and everything for it. And the music was just beautiful, all original things of his. And it's so, I felt so sorry that he passed before it all came to light, you know.
Whatever happened to the music?
I don't know, his daughter had it and you know how those daughters do, if they aren't interested in music and things--
In some trunk probably.

Yeah probably just sitting around all the music, all the dialogue, all the lyrics, everything, just laying there. One of the main things, I was supposed to be in the show, Eddy Bearfield. He says Cozy, what I want to do is get this show going on Broadway, get a big band, he said, and put all my friends to work and let it run. It would have been, the way, I read the whole score, it would have been a Tobacco Road, that kind of show, see and it was the truth in it, way back there, Uncle Tom's Cabin. The name of it was Mr. Tom. And it was the truth and that's what people love to hear, you know, and especially, it would have been ideal now since all those black shows have been on Broadway, Ain't Misbehavin', The Whiz, and things
Bubblin' Brown Sugar.
Yes, see. So it's too bad he had to pass, but that's the way the cookie rolls sometimes.
He died in '77.
Yeah, '77. Edgar Battle.
Very talented man.
Yes, he was.
According to Chilton's book, trumpet, trombone, saxes, piano, organ, as well as arranging and composing.
That's right, arranging and composing. Very talented. Very talented.
Kind of like, well other people like Eddie Wilcox, Andy Gibson.
Yeah Andy Gibson.
Really never got their share of recognition.
Andy Gibson was a good arranger. He arranged for Cab for a while.
For a lot of people.
Oh yeah, for King Records. Eddie Wilcox in there with Jimmy Lunceford.
Oh yeah. You mentioned Eddy Heartfield.
Oh God, he's great, a great musician. I remember when he was on staff at NBC, all the saxophone players wanted to study with Eddie. He's doing, he's teaching

now there at Charlie Coven's studios in New York. And he's also doing a Circus and he just got back, Ivan Rollé told me, bass player from LA, think he did a recording date under his name for the Harry Lim label.
Yeah, I'm told he's playing mostly tenor now.

Yeah, tenor. And Ivan said to me, he says, Oh, Cozy, Eddie's talking about that saxophone's a faggot's instrument.
